query: For Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state, the factors governing its phase stability during cooling and subsequent thermal exposure are not understood well enough to account for the range of phases that may appear. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain this behavior and why? Define a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations relative to that baseline, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: During cooling and subsequent thermal exposure, the high-temperature BCC phase in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 becomes unstable because aluminum, having a higher diffusivity relative to the other elements, segregates and promotes local chemical short‐range order (CSRO). This CSRO then acts as a structural mediator that triggers the nucleation of an ordered/intermetallic phase (e.g., a B2 or similar phase) from the metastable BCC matrix. In contrast, when cooling is rapid (or thermal exposure is brief), the BCC phase is retained due to insufficient time for significant Al segregation and CSRO development.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 in a high-temperature, single-phase BCC state
generation.intervention: Control and vary the cooling rate from the high-temperature state (comparing rapid quenching versus slow cooling) and apply subsequent thermal annealing for defined periods
generation.conditions: The hypothesis applies when cooling rates are sufficiently slow (and/or annealing times are long enough) to allow differential diffusion and segregation of Al. It is not expected to hold under ultrarapid quenching conditions or at temperatures where atomic mobility is uniformly high such that diffusion-controlled segregation is overridden by mixing.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of chemical short‐range order (CSRO) driven by differential diffusivity of aluminum leads to local compositional fluctuations, providing nucleation sites for an ordered (e.g., B2) or intermetallic phase.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism is based on the fact that, during slow cooling and thermal exposure, aluminum atoms diffuse more rapidly than Cr, Co, Fe, and Ni, resulting in localized enrichment and CSRO. This CSRO lowers the nucleation barrier for a secondary ordered phase (or phases) to precipitate from the metastable BCC matrix. In rapid cooling scenarios, insufficient diffusion limits both segregation and the development of CSRO, thereby preserving the high-temperature BCC phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a rapidly quenched sample that remains predominantly single-phase BCC, samples cooled slowly (or thermally aged) will exhibit new diffraction peaks and microstructural features (via TEM/SEM) indicative of an additional ordered/intermetallic phase (e.g., B2 or related structures). The appearance and volume fraction of these phases will correlate with the extent of cooling or annealing exposure.
generation.baseline: A baseline sample prepared by rapid quenching from the high temperature, which, due to minimized atomic diffusion, retains the single-phase BCC structure with little or no evidence of CSRO or secondary phase formation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be valid under conditions where atomic diffusivity is moderate such that aluminum segregation can occur (e.g., slow cooling rates or moderate-temperature annealing). In extremely rapid cooling conditions (e.g., melt-spinning) or at temperatures where diffusion is universally rapid (near melting), other kinetic factors may dominate the transformation behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The specific identity and crystallographic details of the ordered/intermetallic phase(s) that form (e.g., whether it is a typical B2 structure, sigma phase, or another intermetallic) are not fully established and may depend on subtle processing parameters beyond cooling rate and annealing time.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples and subject them to two distinct thermal histories. One set will be rapidly quenched from the high-temperature BCC state (minimal diffusion), while the other set is slowly cooled or subjected to defined thermal annealing steps allowing extended residence time. Characterize both sets using X-ray diffraction (XRD), scanning/transmission electron microscopy (SEM/TEM), and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to assess phase composition and evidence of CSRO or secondary ordered phase formation.
measurements: XRD peak analysis to detect newly emerging ordered/intermetallic phase reflections
TEM/SEM imaging for microstructural evidence of phase separation or precipitate formation
EDS mapping to reveal any localized aluminum enrichment corresponding to CSRO
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slowly cooled and annealed samples do not show any additional ordered or intermetallic phases or evidence of aluminum segregation/CSRO (i.e., they remain indistinguishable from the rapidly quenched baseline BCC state), then the hypothesis that diffusion-driven CSRO mediated phase transformation controls the phase stability is falsified.

The DSC analysis highlights the distinct behavior of first-order phase transitions, characterized by hysteresis where crystallization temperatures are consistently lower than melting temperatures. The weaker thermal anomaly during crystallization, compared to melting, confirms the typical behavior of such transitions []. The heat associated with the dissolution and crystallization of phase “E” is notably higher than that of eutectic transformations, aligning with findings on multicomponent eutectic systems where melting temperatures decrease with increasing alloy complexity []. cited_evidence.text: The equilibrium phase diagram for Fe32Cr33Ni29Al3Ti3 (Figure 12a) shows that solidification begins around 1350 °C with preferential FCC formation. BCC nucleation becomes significant below ~1250 °C. The FCC phase fraction peaks near 1100 °C, consistent with the observed microstructures. To understand phase formation dynamics, temperature–time curves were extracted at four locations: A1, A2 (center), and B1, B2 (bottom) (Figure 11). Table 1 summarizes the residence times in critical temperature intervals (1350–1250 °C and 1250–1100 °C). The bottom locations (B1, B2) experienced shorter times in the 1350–1250 °C range, limiting BCC nucleation. Conversely, the central points (A1, A2) had longer residence times, promoting BCC phase development. However, in the lower energy P160 condition, sharper cooling gradients resulted in a higher BCC phase fraction but a smaller grain size. For P200, prolonged exposure allowed BCC grains to grow larger despite fewer nucleation sites. These results demonstrate how subtle variations in thermal history can modulate the phase content and grain morphology in SLM-processed EHEAs.
